title: BIR suspends controversial QR badge requirement
summary: The BIR stops the mandatory online display of registration badges, which had an original deadline of October 31, following complaints over data privacy and additional red tape

MANILA, Philippines – Online sellers, freelancers, content creators, and other businesses no longer have to display QR-coded tax registration badges on their websites and social media pages after the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) suspended a controversial requirement that had drawn complaints over privacy risks and additional bureaucracy.
BIR Commissioner Charlito Martin Mendoza announced on Monday, October 26, that the requirement would be suspended indefinitely, just five days before the supposed October 31 compliance deadline.
No penalties will be imposed solely for failing to display the badge during the suspension. Those who already have their badges may continue displaying them voluntarily.

The requirement was introduced in April as an alternative to displaying one’s full BIR Certificate of Registration (COR) online. The badge contains a QR code that customers can scan to verify whether an online seller or service provider is registered with the tax bureau.

But what was supposed to make registration verification easier has since sparked debate that QR codes could expose personal information. The rollout was also marred by technical difficulties and confusion over who needed to comply.
“We recognize that protecting personal information online presents different and more complex challenges than displaying a COR at a physical business establishment,” Mendoza said.
The BIR said it would work with the National Privacy Commission and consult affected taxpayers before deciding how to proceed.

Economist and former finance undersecretary Cielo Magno welcomed the suspension but questioned why the requirement was necessary in the first place. Magno pointed out that the BIR already maintains taxpayer registration records and has other mechanisms for monitoring transactions.
She argued that requiring another badge, without clear evidence that it would improve revenue collection, merely adds another administrative burden onto small online sellers and freelancers.
“Instead of encouraging people to enter the formal economy, we risk giving them more reasons to remain outside it,” she said.
Her criticism comes amid longstanding concerns over the Philippines’ complicated business regulations and excessive red tape.

In its latest Business Ready assessment, the World Bank found that Philippine business regulations scored nearly as well as Singapore’s on paper, but the country lagged considerably in implementation. Registering a foreign firm in the Philippines takes 76 days, compared with just one day in Singapore, according to the World Bank.

The international lender has also urged the government to simplify tax compliance, arguing that easier procedures can improve collection by reducing mistakes and encouraging taxpayers to comply voluntarily. – Rappler.com
